name: Dialog
purpose: A modal built on the platform's <dialog>. It interrupts to ask for a decision whose consequences the user should see before making it, and it is the first component in the library that v0 has no version of at all — which is why Move cancels a trip in one press with a driver en route.
responsibilities: Open and close a real <dialog> with showModal(), so the focus trap, the inertness of everything behind it, Escape and the top layer come from the platform.
Name itself. The title is the accessible name, wired with aria-labelledby, and there is no unlabelled variant.
Place initial focus on whichever action is the safe one, after the dialog is open.
Report every route out — the dismissing action, Escape, and the backdrop — through one callback.
Nothing about what confirming means. It renders two labels and calls two handlers.
Nothing about its own visibility. open is controlled, and the component never closes itself without saying so.
do: Name the verb in both labels. "Cancel trip" and "Keep trip", never "Yes" and "No", and never "Cancel" in a dialog about cancelling something — it reads as either answer.

Put the consequence in description. It is announced on open through aria-describedby, and it is where the weight of a destructive action goes now that decision 020 has refused a destructive Button variant.
Leave confirmIsSafe false for anything irreversible, so a user who presses Enter out of habit keeps what they had.
Set confirmIsSafe true only where confirming cannot hurt — a retry, a save-before-leaving.
Open it from a real control, so the browser has somewhere to return focus when it closes.
dont: Do not use the open attribute instead of showModal(). <dialog open> is a NON-modal dialog — no top layer, no focus trap, nothing inert, no Escape — and it looks identical on screen.

Do not draw anything on the scrim. Decision 025 gives surface.scrim no contrast pairing, because check-contrast.mjs refuses to measure a translucent background, and the rule that makes that safe is that nothing is read through it.
Do not use a dialog for something that is not a decision. A modal takes the whole screen away; a message that can be read and ignored is not one.

Do not make either action primary. A primary fill on the destructive choice is the refused variant arriving under another name, and a primary on the safe one pushes an answer at somebody who may want the other.
Do not animate it in. A dialog that fades is a dialog whose first frames are spent not being usable, and it delays the moment a keyboard user's focus is somewhere predictable.
Do not remove the way out. dismissLabel is required and Escape is never intercepted.

do_not_use_when.when: The message needs no decision and can be read and ignored — a save confirmation, a background sync finishing.
do_not_use_when.use_instead: Nothing yet. A toast or an inline status region is the shape, and neither exists; both are less interrupting than this by design.

do_not_use_when.when: The content is a whole task rather than a question — a full form, a checkout step, a filter panel.
do_not_use_when.use_instead: A page or a route. A modal that contains a task is a page with the browser's back button taken away.

do_not_use_when.when: The dialog would need to open another dialog.
do_not_use_when.use_instead: A single dialog whose content changes, or a route. Stacked modals leave a user with no model of where they are and no reliable way back.

do_not_use_when.when: Something must be drawn on the backdrop itself.
do_not_use_when.use_instead: Nothing. Give it an opaque ground inside the dialog — the scrim carries no contrast guarantee and a control on it would be unmeasurable.

do_not_use_when.when: The action is trivially reversible and the interruption buys nothing.
do_not_use_when.use_instead: Just doing it, with an undo. A confirmation nobody reads trains people to dismiss the one that matters.

alternatives.for: the action itself, when it needs no confirmation
a whole task rather than a question

alternatives.use: an inline status region or a toast
alternatives.for: a message that needs no decision

content: The title, which asks the question or states what happened.
The description, which is where the consequence goes — the sentence that makes a destructive action a real decision.
The two labels, each naming what will happen rather than agreeing or disagreeing.
constraints: No width and no fixed height. The dialog is sized against the viewport with a readable ceiling, never in fixed pixels.
No destructive variant, no tone and no icon. Decision 020 refused the variant and the token layer has no action-danger semantic; this component works around neither.
No colour that content/tokens/pairs.json has not seen — with one deliberate exception argued in decision 025, the scrim, which carries no pairing because a translucent background cannot be measured.
No entrance animation. Decision 021's scale exists and is deliberately not reached for.
No way to suppress the dismissing action or intercept Escape.
No focus management beyond placing the initial focus. The trap and the restoration are the platform's.

Three written numbers, counted exactly rather than rounded to one: the 1px edge (fifth time in the library, still no border-width scale); 28rem, the readable ceiling on the dialog's width; and 26rem, the width below which the actions stretch — which is the library's first viewport-dimension media query and therefore a breakpoint in a system with no breakpoint scale, flagged rather than smoothed.

behaviour: The actions sit at the reading END of their row through justify-content: flex-end, which is a position on the inline axis rather than a physical edge, so the row flips with the document.
The dismissing action is first in reading order and the committing action last, in both directions. Last is the last thing read before acting.

The title and description carry dir="auto" as blocks, on the same §3 reasoning Input records: <bdi> isolates a run inside a sentence, but alignment belongs to the block, and this component cannot read a ReactNode.
Arabic line height on the title, because §6 measured مُخفَّض reaching above the font's declared ascent and a short heading is exactly where a tight leading looks safe and clips.
letter-spacing 0, always. There is no [dir='rtl'] selector anywhere.

Below a narrow breakpoint the actions stretch rather than huddling at one end, because §6 measured Arabic running to 117 per cent of English on some strings and a wrapped row of end-aligned buttons reads as a mistake.
mirrors: The whole dialog, with the document.
The action row, which flips as a unit while keeping its reading order.
does_not_mirror: Nothing. There is no glyph in this component whose form carries meaning.

guarantees: A real <dialog> opened with showModal(), so the focus trap, the inertness of the rest of the page, Escape and the top layer are the platform's rather than a re-implementation's.
An accessible name, always. title is required and wired with aria-labelledby.
The consequence is announced on open, through aria-describedby on the description.

Initial focus lands on the safe action, placed after showModal() rather than with React's autoFocus — which silently does nothing here, because React focuses at mount and mount happens while the dialog is still closed.
Escape, the backdrop and the dismissing action are one event, so the way out is the same whichever a user reaches for.
Focus returns to whatever opened the dialog when it closes. That restoration is the platform's and is the reason to open one from a real control.
0 axe violations across all seven stories, checked in dark + RTL.
consumer_must: Open the dialog from a real focusable control, or the browser has nowhere to return focus on close.
Write labels that name the verb. The component cannot check that "Yes" is a worse label than "Cancel trip", and the whole safety argument rests on the words.
Decide confirmIsSafe honestly. It moves where a habitual Enter lands, and defaulting it to true for convenience is how a confirmation stops being one.
Keep the dialog's content to a decision. Nothing prevents a whole form being passed as children, and a modal containing a task is a page with the back button removed.

props.name: children
props.description: Anything more than a sentence. Most dialogs should not need it.
props.guidance: Anything more than a sentence, and most dialogs should not need it. A modal that contains a task is a page with the back button removed.

props.name: confirmIsSafe
props.description: Whether confirming is the safe choice.
notes: It decides **where focus lands when the dialog opens**, and nothing else — no colour, no icon, no variant. Defaults to `false`, which is the cautious reading: a dialog that had to be built usually exists because the action behind it is worth a second thought, so focus goes to the dismissing action and a user who hits Enter out of habit keeps what they had.
Set it `true` where the confirming action is the harmless one — "Save before leaving?", "Retry?" — so that habit lands on the outcome the user almost certainly wants.
props.guidance: Decides where initial focus lands and nothing else. Defaults to false, which is the cautious reading: a dialog that had to be built usually exists because the action behind it is worth a second thought.

props.name: confirmLabel
props.description: The label on the confirming action. Omit it — along with {@link DialogProps.onConfirm} — for a dialog that only has to be acknowledged.
notes: **Name the verb.** `Cancel trip` and `Keep trip`, not `Yes` and `No`. Decision 020 refused a destructive Button variant and said the weight of an action lives in the label; this is the component where that stops being a principle and becomes the only mechanism available.
props.guidance: Name the verb. Omit it, with onConfirm, for a dialog that only has to be acknowledged.

props.name: description
props.description: The consequence, in a sentence. Linked with `aria-describedby`, so it is announced when the dialog opens rather than only seen.
notes: This is where the weight of a destructive action goes — see the component docs. "Your driver is two minutes away" is what makes "Cancel trip" a real decision rather than a button somebody presses to make a box go away.
props.guidance: The consequence, announced on open. This is where the weight of a destructive action lives now that decision 020 has refused a destructive variant — "Your driver is two minutes away" is a stronger signal than any colour, and it reaches a colour-blind user.

props.name: dismissLabel
props.description: The label on the dismissing action. **Required**, because there is always a way out — see {@link DialogProps.onDismiss}.
notes: Say what not-doing-it means rather than "Cancel", which is ambiguous in exactly the dialog where ambiguity is most expensive: "Cancel" in a *cancel-the-trip* dialog can be read as either answer.
props.guidance: Required, because there is always a way out. Say what not-doing-it means: "Cancel" is ambiguous in exactly the dialog where ambiguity is most expensive.

props.name: onConfirm
props.description: Called when the confirming action is pressed.
props.guidance: Called by the committing action. The component has no opinion about what it does.

props.name: onDismiss
props.description: Called when the dialog should close: the dismissing action, the Escape key, or a click on the backdrop.
notes: All three routes are the same event on purpose. A dialog that can be escaped by one route and not another teaches a user that the box is unpredictable, and Escape is the one everybody already knows.
props.guidance: Called by the dismissing action, Escape and the backdrop alike. One event for three routes, because a dialog that can be escaped one way and not another teaches a user that the box is unpredictable.

props.name: open
props.description: Whether the dialog is showing. Controlled — the consumer owns the state, and this component never closes itself without saying so through {@link DialogProps.onDismiss}.
props.guidance: Controlled. The component never closes itself without reporting it, so the prop and the DOM cannot drift — which is exactly what happens if Escape is left unhandled, because the element closes in its own eyes and the next open={true} is a no-op.

props.name: title
props.description: What the dialog is asking or telling. Required, rendered as a real `<h2>`, and wired as the dialog's accessible name with `aria-labelledby`.
notes: There is no `aria-label` escape hatch and no unlabelled variant. A modal takes the whole screen away from someone; arriving in one with no name is arriving somewhere with no idea what it is.
props.guidance: The accessible name, via aria-labelledby, and a real <h2>. Required: a modal takes the whole screen away, and arriving in one with no name is arriving somewhere with no idea what it is.

unmapped.why: Whether a dialog is showing is a state of the screen rather than a property of the component. A Figma file draws the open one; the closed one is the screen without it.
A handler is behaviour. Figma properties describe what a component looks like.
It moves initial focus and changes no pixel. A Figma variant for it would be two identical frames.
Arbitrary content has no property to mirror. In Figma it is a slot the designer fills directly.

use_when: An action is irreversible and the user should see the consequence before committing.
A decision must be made before anything else can continue.
Something has happened that has to be acknowledged before the screen is usable again.
not_a: A toast or an inline message. Those do not need a decision and do not take the screen away.
A page. A modal containing a whole task is a page with the back button removed.
A component with a destructive variant. There is no red button here and its absence is a decision.
A place to draw something on the backdrop.

deprecation.policy: The second component in the library with no v0 predecessor, so it is withdrawn only by a decision naming what replaces it. A prop is withdrawn ahead of the component: mark it @deprecated in the source with the replacement named in the tag, keep it working for one minor version, then remove it in a major one with the migration written down. confirmIsSafe is the prop most likely to move — if the answer ever needs to be "neither", that is a third state on one prop rather than a second prop, for the reason decision 020 gives about v0's three names for one axis.
